more patients who previously would only have been candidates for CABG being treated by percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Increasingly, the favorable results obtained with DES mean that PCI is performed in complex cases such as LMCA stenosis, diffuse disease, and bifurcation anatomy.
Several large RCTs, which have demonstrated both the safety and efﬁ  -
cacy of these stents, have supported the introduction of DES into routine clinical practice.
 Sirolimus-eluting stents
The drug sirolimus has potent antifungal, immunosuppressive, and antimi-totic properties. This agent was approved for rejection prophylaxis in renal transplantation in 1999, with trials of a sirolimus-coated coronary stent following soon thereafter.
The ﬁ  rst human experience of a sirolimus-coated stent (45 patients) • 
illustrated a virtual absence of neoinitimal proliferation at follow-up.
 Box 14.4 Drug-eluting stents
Similarities between tumor growth and benign neointimal • 
proliferation introduced the concept that immunosuppressant and cytotoxic agents might be beneﬁ  cial for preventing in-stent restenosis.Incorporation of these agents into stent coatings, using a number of • 
techniques, has now enabled delivery of the active agent directly to its site of action, while limiting systemic side effects.Crucially, the coatings allow sustained release of the agent such • 
that the therapy is present at the time that the target mechanism is physiologically active.The commonly used agents are sirolimus, which has a cytostatic • 
action, and paclitaxel, which is cytotoxic. Other agents include everolimus and zatorolimus. DRUG-ELUTING STENTS 575
The seminal RAVEL study enrolled 238 patients, randomly allocated to • 
BX velocity stent, or sirolimus-eluting BX velocity stent (the Cypher™ Stent). It reported 0% restenosis in the group treated with the DES.The large-scale SIRIUS study (• n = 1100) conﬁ  rmed the potent 
antirestenosis effects of Cypher™ stents.
  Paclitaxel eluting stents
Paclitaxel has potent antitumor activity via its action as a microtubule-stabilizing agent. Coronary stents eluting paclitaxel have been extensively investigated.
TAXUS I studied 61 patients randomly assigned to paclitaxel-coated • 
stent or bare metal stent. This study both established the safety of the stent, but also showed a major adverse cardiac events (MACE) rate in the DES arm of 3%, compared with 10% in the BMS arm at 1-year follow-up.TAXUS II compared slow- and moderate-release formulations of • 
paclitaxel with bare metal stenting, and found signiﬁ  cantly lower 
MACE rates in both slow- and moderate-release DES (2.3%/4.7%) than those in BMS-treated control groups (20.2%).
SIRIUS and TAXUS, and each of their subsequent follow-up studies and registries, have established that Cypher™ and Taxus™ stents have similar, low rates of TLR (between 3% and 8%).
 Box 14.5 
AHA/ACC/ESC recommends the use of a DES in PCI for patients with symptomatic CAD in whom the target artery is <3 mm in caliber or the lesion is longer than 15 mm. In real-world practice this translates to coronary artery lesions in approximately 60%–70% of patients under-going PCI.

   Stent thrombosis
It should be appreciated that documentation of ST by angiography under-estimates the real incidence of this event, since some of the patients with stent thrombosis develop MI or die without angiographic documentation of stent thrombosis.
To address this issue, an Academic Research Consortium (ARC) com-
posed of clinical investigators, industry representatives, and regulatory authorities (including the FDA) has proposed new deﬁ  nitions for ST in an attempt to establish uniformity and improve sensitivity for the diagnosis of ST.
There are three levels of evidence in deﬁ  ning ST:
1. Deﬁ  nite stent thrombosisAngiographic conﬁ  rmation is based on TIMI (thrombolysis in myocardial infarction) ﬂ  ow:
TIMI ﬂ  ow 0 with occlusion originating in the stent or in the segment • 
5 mm proximal or distal to the stent region with presence of thrombusTIMI ﬂ  ow 1, 2, or 3 originating in the stent or the segment 5 mm • 
proximal or distal to the stent region with presence of thrombus
AND at least one of the following criteria has been fulﬁ  lled within a 48-hours period:
New acute onset of ischemic symptoms at rest• 
New ischemic electrocardiogram changes that suggest acute ischemia• 
Typical rise and fall in cardiac biomarkers as evidence for an acute MI• Pathologic conﬁ  rmation
Conﬁ  rmation of recent ST either at autopsy or via examination of • 
tissue retrieved after thrombectomy
2. Probable stent thrombosisConsidered to have occurred after intracoronary stent implantation in the following cases:
Any unexplained death within the ﬁ  rst 30 days• 
Irrespective of the time after the index procedure, any MI that is • 
related to acute ischemia in the territory of the implanted stent without angiographic conﬁ  rmation of stent thrombosis and in the absence of any other obvious cause
3. Possible stent thrombosis
Any unexplained death from 30 days after intracoronary stenting until • 
end of trial follow-up
Based on the timing after implantation of DES, ST could be
Acute: 0 to 24 hours post–stent implantation• 
Subacute: 24 hours to 30 days post–stent implantation• 
Late: 30 days to 1 year post–stent implantation• 
Very late: >1 year post–stent implantation•

nodes.title: Stent thrombosis
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses stent thrombosis (ST) in the context of cardiac catheterization, highlighting the underestimation of its incidence due to cases where patients experience myocardial infarction (MI) or death without angiographic evidence of ST. It introduces new definitions proposed by the Academic Research Consortium (ARC) to standardize and enhance the sensitivity of ST diagnosis. The document outlines three levels of evidence for defining ST: 

1. **Definite Stent Thrombosis** - Requires angiographic confirmation with specific TIMI flow criteria and at least one acute ischemic symptom or biomarker rise within 48 hours.
2. **Probable Stent Thrombosis** - Includes unexplained deaths within 30 days post-implantation or MIs related to the stent territory without angiographic confirmation.
3. **Possible Stent Thrombosis** - Refers to unexplained deaths occurring from 30 days post-implantation until the end of trial follow-up.

Additionally, it categorizes ST based on the timing after drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation into acute, subacute, late, and very late phases.

Based on the design of the pivotal clinical trials that led to approval of DES, dual antiplatelet therapy was prescribed on an empirical basis for 2–3 months after implantation of sirolimus-eluting stents and for 6 months after implantation of paclitaxel-eluting stents, with lifelong aspirin.
However, concerns about long-term safety were ﬁ  rst made public 
in 2005 after several case reports were published that suggested that even late after DES placement, discontinuation of antiplatelet therapy may allow stent thrombosis. This appears to be due to failure of DES to re-endothelialize.
These concerns were conﬁ  rmed when 746 nonselected patients with 
1133 stented lesions surviving 6 months without major events were fol-lowed for 1 year after the discontinuation of clopidogrel in the BASKET-LATE trial, which showed that documented late stent thrombosis and related death/target vessel MI were twice as frequent after DES vs. BMS (2.6% vs. 1.3%). Thrombosis-related events occurred between 15 and 362 days after the discontinuation of clopidogrel, presenting as MI or death in 88% of the cases.
Since then, multiple trials, registries, and meta-analyses have studied the 
incidence of DES ST with numbers that range from 0.4% to 2.9%. Based on these data, the FDA now recommends continuous use of dual antiplatelet therapy for 1–2 years if there are not major bleeding complications.CHAPTER 14 Cardiac catheterization 578
  Physiological assessment of coronary ﬂ ow
The shortcomings of coronary angiography in the physiological assessment 
of coronary stenosis are clear. Intravascular ultrasound can provide infor-mation on the size of the lumen and the composition of plaque, but again gives no information on the effect that an atheromatous plaque may have on coronary ﬂ  ow. The knowledge as to whether a narrowing seen on angiography is the culprit causing hemodynamic effects, and thus anginal symptoms, is valuable when guiding percutaneous intervention.
The fractional ﬂ  ow reserve (FFR) correlates distal coronary pressure to 
myocardial blood ﬂ  ow during maximum hyperemia (induced by infusion of adenosine, or papaverine). FFR is deﬁ  ned as maximum myocardial blood ﬂ ow in the presence of a stenosis divided by the theoretical maximum 
ﬂ  ow in the absence of a stenosis (see Fig. 14.13).
Thus the information derived from FFR allows an “on-the-spot” diag-
nosis of the extent to which a given stenosis contributes to myocardial ischemia (and angina), and can guide decisions regarding revascularization. At present, the best established indication for coronary FFR estimation is as a diagnostic tool to assess “severe” coronary stenosis, and for this it is extremely sensitive when used with a cutoff point of 0.75. The technique has also been used to optimize the results of stent implantation.
Two technologies are currently available that provide hemodynamic 
information derived from FFR calculations; these are pressure wires (which consist of a pressure transducer mounted on a 0.014” guide wire), and Doppler ﬂ  ow wires (which examine coronary ﬂ  ow velocities using spectral analysis).Pressure wire, e.g., the PressureWire™ (Radi Medical Systems, Volcano Medical Systems)
The pressure transducer is located at the transition between the • 
radiopaque wire tip and the nonradiopaque stem.The analyzer shows simultaneous aortic and intracoronary pressure, as • 
well as instantaneous FFR.
Doppler wire, e.g., FlowWire™ (Endosonics)
This obtains information on coronary ﬂ  ow velocity in the central area • 
of the arterial lumen.Combining ﬂ  ow and ECG information, it calculates systolic and • 
diastolic components of ﬂ  ow velocity at baseline.Following induction of hyperemia, the machine can calculate the • 
coronary ﬂ  ow velocity reserve.

The partial document covers two main topics related to cardiac catheterization: the physiological assessment of coronary flow and primary angioplasty for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). 

1. **Physiological Assessment of Coronary Flow**: It discusses the limitations of coronary angiography in evaluating coronary stenosis and highlights the importance of fractional flow reserve (FFR) in assessing the hemodynamic impact of stenosis on myocardial blood flow. FFR is defined as the ratio of maximum myocardial blood flow in the presence of a stenosis to the theoretical maximum flow without stenosis. The document describes two technologies for measuring FFR: pressure wires and Doppler flow wires, detailing their functions and how they provide hemodynamic information.

2. **Primary Angioplasty for STEMI**: The document explains the pathophysiology of STEMI, emphasizing the urgency of restoring coronary blood flow to prevent myocardial damage. It outlines the preferred treatment method, primary angioplasty, which involves urgent coronary arteriography and stent implantation. The text also compares primary angioplasty with other reperfusion strategies, such as intravenous fibrinolysis and rescue angioplasty, noting their effectiveness and limitations in achieving full arterial patency.

  Primary angioplasty for STEMI
 Pathophysiology
In the context of cardiac chest pain, ST segment elevation on the 12 lead ECG usually signiﬁ  es complete occlusion of a proximal epicardial coronary artery. This occurs as a result of rupture or erosion of a vulnerable athero-matous plaque, which leads to platelet activation and adhesion, formation of platelet-rich (white) thrombus, ﬁ  brin deposition, and red cell entrap-ment (forming red thrombus).
If untreated, myocardial necrosis commences within 30 minutes, affect-
ing full myocardial thickness within 6 hours; 30% of patients die before reaching the hospital.
  Treatment
Urgent restoration of coronary blood ﬂ  ow (reperfusion) prevents further 
LV damage and improves prognosis (Box 14.6). The amount of myocar-dium that can be salvaged falls exponentially with time, with the greatest beneﬁ  t within 3 hours following symptom onset, and little beneﬁ  t after 
12 hours.Primary angioplasty is the preferred reperfusion strategy, where angiography can be performed within 90 minutes of presentation.Patients can be transferred safely (by a trained ambulance crew with an ACLS trained escort) from a community hospital to a cardiac center for primary angioplasty.
 Box 14.6 Options for reperfusion
Primary angioplastyImmediate coronary arteriography, culprit vessel angioplasty, and stent implantation without antecedent ﬁ  brinolysis achieves full arterial patency 
(TIMI grade 3 ﬂ  ow) in 90%–95%, treating the occlusive thrombus and the culprit plaque.Intravenous ﬁ  brinolysis
Immediate administration of a ﬁ  brinolytic agent (also called thrombolysis) 
without planned coronary arteriography achieves full arterial patency (TIMI grade 3 ﬂ  ow) in 50%–60%. It is contraindicated in up to 30% of patients and does not treat the culprit plaque.Rescue angioplastyUrgent coronary arteriography, culprit vessel angioplasty, and stent implantation are performed when ﬁ  brinolysis has failed to achieve reperfusion (persistent ST-segment elevation 9 pain at 60–90 minutes).

Pre-procedure preparations are listed, including necessary consents, blood work, and medications. The document also mentions the importance of identifying the culprit vessel during the diagnostic angiogram and the criteria for procedural success. Additional considerations regarding the management of non-infarct-related arteries are also addressed.

nodes.title: Invasive assessment of vulnerable plaque
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses the invasive assessment of vulnerable atherosclerotic plaques, highlighting the risks associated with non-obstructive plaques that can lead to myocardial infarction. It emphasizes the limitations of traditional angiography in differentiating between stable and vulnerable plaques, prompting the development of advanced imaging technologies. Key points include:

1. **Histopathological Features of Vulnerable Plaque**: Characteristics such as lipid-rich cores, thin fibrous caps, necrotic cores, and high macrophage infiltration are identified as indicators of vulnerability.

2. **Intravascular Ultrasound (IVUS)**: This technique can differentiate between plaque types based on echodensity and identify rupture areas, providing a histological map when combined with image analysis.

3. **Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Similar to IVUS but using light, OCT offers high-resolution anatomical information, though its functional correlation is still under investigation.

4. **Intravascular Elastography**: This method uses sound waves to assess plaque material properties, helping to identify areas of increased strain that may lead to rupture.

5. **Chronic Total Occlusion (CTO)**: The document outlines the definition, challenges, and techniques for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in treating CTOs, emphasizing the importance of guide wire advancement and stent implantation.

6. **Bifurcation Lesions**: It defines bifurcation lesions and discusses the implications of plaque extension into side branches, advocating for a provisional stenting technique over dual stenting to minimize complications.

7. **Drug-Eluting Stents (DES)**: Recent findings suggest that DES can reduce restenosis and reintervention rates in bifurcation treatments.

Overall, the document provides insights into advanced imaging techniques and interventional strategies for managing vulnerable plaques and complex coronary lesions.

   Complex coronary angioplasty
 Chronic total occlusion
Chronic total occlusion (CTO) is deﬁ  ned as a completely occluded coron-
ary artery, with the occlusion being known to have been present for >3 months. The age and length of the occlusion are the main determinants of success of PCI (e.g., see Box 14.7). The objectives in treating CTOs per-cutaneously are as follows:
Crossing of the total occlusion with a guide wire and advancement of • 
this wire into the distal vessel (inability to cross with the guide wire is the reason for failure in 50% of attempts at CTO PCI)Dilatation of the underlying occlusion• 
Preservation of the newly recanalized lumen by the implantation of a • 
stent and by pharmacological means
 Techniques that may improve success
Aggressive guide catheter support, including deep cannulation of the • 
coronary arteryOver-the-wire balloon to support the guide wire as it is advanced • 
against the CTOStiffer guide wires that require greater forces to deﬂ  ect the tip and • 
may be more successful in penetrating the “cap” of the CTO. Great care must be taken with guide wires of this nature, as there is risk of perforation of the target vessel.
Unfortunately, if the lumen is recanalized, the rates of reocclusion are high, even when the CTO is stented.
   Bifurcation lesions
A simple deﬁ  nition of bifurcation lesions can be the involvement of a side branch with a reference diameter >2 mm in the stenosis. IVUS studies show that plaque in the main vessel almost invariably extends some dis-tance into side branches that arise within the plaque. Furthermore, angi-oplasty to a plaque will often cause plaque shift (the so-called snow plow effect) into the daughter vessel.

nodes.title: Bifurcation lesions
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers advanced techniques and considerations in cardiac catheterization, specifically focusing on complex coronary angioplasty. Key points include:

1. **Chronic Total Occlusion (CTO)**: Defined as a completely occluded coronary artery present for over three months, with success in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) dependent on the age and length of the occlusion. The main objectives in treating CTOs include crossing the occlusion with a guide wire, dilating the occlusion, and preserving the lumen with stenting.

2. **Techniques to Improve Success**: Emphasizes the use of aggressive guide catheter support, over-the-wire balloons, and stiffer guide wires, while noting the risks associated with these methods, such as vessel perforation and high rates of reocclusion post-recanalization.

3. **Bifurcation Lesions**: Discusses the definition and implications of bifurcation lesions, the preference for provisional stenting techniques over dual stenting, and the risks associated with balloon dilation through stent struts. It highlights the benefits of drug-eluting stents (DES) in reducing restenosis and reintervention rates.

4. **Complex Angioplasty Considerations**: Lists factors that complicate angioplasty, including patient characteristics and lesion characteristics, which can increase procedural failure risk and affect long-term outcomes.

5. **Left Main Stem Angioplasty**: Reviews guidelines suggesting bypass surgery for left main coronary artery stenosis, while acknowledging that PCI can be acceptable in certain cases with low complication rates. It discusses the role of DES in improving outcomes and the importance of achieving excellent angiographic results, with follow-up angiography recommended to monitor for restenosis. 

Overall, the document provides a detailed overview of the complexities and evolving strategies in coronary angioplasty, particularly for challenging cases like CTOs and bifurcation lesions.

AHA/ACC/ESC guidelines suggest that patients with stenosis of the left main coronary artery should be offered bypass graft surgery. However, the registry data for both bare metal stents and, more recently, drug-eluting stents have suggested that PCI to the left main stem (LMS) in patients with suitable LMS anatomy achieves acceptable results with low rates of procedural complication and long-term vessel patency. in-stent restenosis with DES than with BMS have further changed the approach of many interventional cardiologists to this previously taboo subset. nodes.title: Left main stem angioplasty
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses cardiac catheterization, specifically focusing on left main stem (LMS) angioplasty and adjunctive therapies for angioplasty and stenting. It highlights the American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC), and European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommending bypass graft surgery for patients with left main coronary artery stenosis, while also noting that percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) can be acceptable in certain cases with suitable anatomy. The document outlines patient groups for whom LMS PCI may be appropriate, including those at high risk for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), patients who refuse surgery, and younger patients with favorable anatomy. It emphasizes the importance of achieving excellent angiographic results and the use of intravascular ultrasound for optimal outcomes. 

Additionally, the document covers adjunctive therapies for angioplasty and stenting, detailing the roles of aspirin, thienopyridines (like clopidogrel), heparin, and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in enhancing procedural outcomes and reducing complications. It discusses the recommended dosages and timing for these medications, as well as the importance of dual antiplatelet therapy in improving patient outcomes during and after PCI.

Most operators routinely reexamine the LMS by angiography 6–9 
months after PCI to look for restenosis.ADJUNCTIVE THERAPY FOR ANGIOPLASTY AND STENTING 587
  Adjunctive therapy for angioplasty and stenting
 Aspirin
The beneﬁ  cial effect of aspirin during PCI has been shown in multiple trials, in which treatment with aspirin and dipyridamole was superior to placebo in the prevention of periprocedural Q-wave MI.
Subsequent studies have shown that dipyridamole added nothing to the 
beneﬁ  cial effects provided by aspirin. Aspirin (usually 325 mg once daily), 
initiated at least 24 hours prior to procedure, is recommended in patients undergoing elective PCI.
  Thienopyridines
Clopidogrel and ticlopidine are thienopyridine derivatives that inhibit platelet function independent of aspirin by interference with the platelet ADP receptor. Early studies showed that a dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticlopidine was superior to aspirin alone. The use of ticlopidine is limited by its side effects, including severe neutropenia.
Clopidogrel, a newer thienopyridine, with a safer side-effect proﬁ  le, 
has thus become the agent of choice. The PCI-CURE study showed that pre-treatment with clopidogrel (300 mg loading dose, followed by 75 mg daily) in addition to aspirin for a median of 10 days before percutaneous coronary intervention, compared with aspirin alone, reduced the compos-ite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or urgent target vessel revascularization by 30% after 1 month.
Most centers have adopted the policy of high loading dose clopidogrel 
(600 mg 2–4 hours pre-PCI) if the patient has not been preloaded.
  Heparin
Although there is general agreement that patients undergoing PCI should 
receive heparin before the intervention, there remains controversy regard-ing the issue of optimal heparin dosage. An inverse relation between the level
 of anticoagulation (measured by activated clotting time [ACT]) 
and the occurrence of acute ischemic complications has been observed. However, longer ACTs are associated with higher bleeding risks.
Currently, an ACT of 250–300 seconds is recommended for patients 
undergoing PCI. Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) has been shown to be effective in PCI, although it has not yet replaced unfraction-ated heparin in routine use.
  Glycoprotein IIb/IIa inhibitors
The ﬁ  nal common pathway for platelet aggregation is mediated by the platelet glycoprotein (gp) IIb/IIIa receptor. Trials in both diabetics and nondiabetics undergoing percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty have found that the combination of stenting and a gpIIb/IIIa inhibitor reduces cardiovascular morbidity and mortality compared with stent plus placebo.

nodes.title: Adjunctive therapy for angioplasty and stenting
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses adjunctive therapies for angioplasty and stenting, focusing on various medications and devices used to enhance patient outcomes during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Key points include:

1. **Aspirin**: Highlighted as a critical medication for preventing periprocedural myocardial infarction (MI), with recommendations for its use at least 24 hours prior to elective PCI.

2. **Thienopyridines**: Clopidogrel and ticlopidine are discussed, with clopidogrel being preferred due to its safer side-effect profile. Evidence from the PCI-CURE study supports the use of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel to reduce cardiovascular events.

3. **Heparin**: The document addresses the use of heparin during PCI, noting the debate over optimal dosing and the recommended activated clotting time (ACT) for balancing efficacy and bleeding risk.

4. **Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa Inhibitors**: These agents are mentioned as effective in reducing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality when used in conjunction with stenting.

5. **Bivalirudin**: A direct thrombin inhibitor that has shown comparable benefits to traditional therapies while reducing the risk of significant bleeding.

6. **Embolic Protection Devices**: The document emphasizes the importance of these devices in preventing distal embolization during PCI, which can lead to complications. It describes two main types: balloon occlusion devices and filter devices, detailing their mechanisms and potential limitations.

Overall, the document provides a comprehensive overview of adjunctive therapies and devices aimed at improving the safety and efficacy of angioplasty and stenting procedures.

  Bivalirudin
Bivalirudin is a direct thrombin inhibitor that exerts its activity by speciﬁ  -
cally and reversibly interacting with circulating (inactive) and clot-bound (active) thrombin.
Clinical trials in patients with stable or unstable angina or acute myocar-

   Embolic protection devices
The distal embolization of particulate matter that lodges in the microcir-culation (e.g., plaque debris, thrombus, and ﬁ  brin) during balloon inﬂ  ation 
and stent deployment is becoming increasingly recognized as a cause of suboptimal results after PCI. Distal embolization leads to poor ﬂ  ow in the proximal vessel undergoing intervention due to occlusion of distal micro-vasculature, the “no-reﬂ  ow” phenomenon.
Vein grafts, and thrombotic lesions are now recognized as being par-
ticularly prone to complications arising from distal embolization, which is seen in up to 30% of vein grafts (these often contain thrombus at the time of PCI). Hence the use of distal protection devices should be considered in these angioplasty subsets.
 Devices for distal protection
Devices can be broadly split into those that occlude the conduit distally and then allow aspiration of debris, or distal ﬁ  lters that capture debris downstream. Balloon occlusion devices
PercuSurge GuardWire. This consists of three parts:• 
1. The GuardWire temporary occlusion catheter, which is placed 
distally in the vessel to allow occlusion.
2. The MicroSeal adapter, which allows control over the inﬂ  ation and 
deﬂ  ation of the balloon.
3. The Export aspiration catheter, which allows collected debris to be 
aspirated into a 20 mL syringe.
One of the main disadvantages of this system is that the target vessel is temporarily occluded, thus the distal myocardium may be rendered ischemic.  Filter devices
AngioGuard. This device consists of an angioplasty guide wire with an • 
expandable ﬁ  lter at the distal tip. The ﬁ  lter can be expanded once the 
target lesion has been crossed. Anterograde blood ﬂ  ow in the vessel is maintained, and displaced debris should theoretically be collected in the ﬁ  lter. The ﬁ  lter is then collapsed and withdrawn into the retrieving catheter.FilterWire EZ™ (Fig. 14.16). This device consists of a “ﬁ  sh mouth” • 
opening distal ﬁ  lter, mounted on an angioplasty guide wire. The “mouth” of the ﬁ  lter in theory expands to ﬁ  ll the entire lumen of the vessel. The ﬁ  lter is deployed by withdrawing a delivery sheath, and collected into a retrieval sheath.
   Limitations of distal protection devices
Crossing proﬁ  le may cause distal embolization• 
Incomplete ﬁ  lter apposition or incomplete conduit occlusion• 
Lack of protection of side branches• 
Distal ischemia in balloon occlusion devices•

nodes.title: Embolic protection devices
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses embolic protection devices used during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to prevent distal embolization of particulate matter, which can lead to suboptimal outcomes and the "no-reflow" phenomenon. It highlights the risks associated with distal embolization, particularly in vein grafts and thrombotic lesions, and emphasizes the importance of using distal protection devices in these cases. The document categorizes these devices into two main types: balloon occlusion devices, such as the PercuSurge GuardWire, which temporarily occlude the vessel to allow for debris aspiration, and filter devices, like AngioGuard and FilterWire EZ™, which capture debris while maintaining blood flow. Limitations of these devices are also noted, including potential distal embolization during crossing, incomplete filter apposition, lack of protection for side branches, and ischemia caused by balloon occlusion. Additionally, the document introduces thrombectomy devices designed to aspirate debris and thrombus, such as the Transluminal Extraction Catheter (TEC), Export catheter, and Angiojet, which utilize different mechanisms for debris removal.

nodes.title: Thrombectomy
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses two main medical procedures: thrombectomy and percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (PMV). 

In the thrombectomy section, it highlights the development of devices designed to aspirate debris and thrombus, including the Transluminal Extraction Catheter (TEC), Export Catheter, and Angiojet, each with unique mechanisms and limitations. 

The PMV section outlines its role as the preferred treatment for symptomatic patients with moderate to severe mitral stenosis, emphasizing the importance of careful case selection based on factors such as age, valve morphology, presence of mitral regurgitation, and left atrial thrombus. It notes that older patients may have poorer outcomes and that a valve scoring system is used to evaluate suitability for the procedure. Additionally, it mentions that PMV can be performed during pregnancy with reduced radiation risk after 14 weeks.

In carefully selected patients with mitral stenosis, percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty (PMV) (see Fig. 14.17) is now the treatment of choice, according to the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology:

ered the initial procedure of choice for symptomatic patients with mod-erate to severe mitral stenosis who have favorable valve morphology in the absence of signiﬁ  cant mitral regurgitation or left atrial thrombus. even in the presence of suboptimal valve morphology.  Valve morphologyA valve scoring system (an echocardiogram-based evaluation of valve cal-ciﬁ cation and anatomy) is used to assess the valves suitability for PMV: 
leaﬂ et mobility, leaﬂ  et thickening, valve calciﬁ  cation, and involvement 
of the subvalvular apparatus. Each parameter evaluated receives from 0 (none) to 4 (severe).

achieve superior and more sustained results from the procedure than patients with scores >8.  Mitral regurgitationThe presence of signiﬁ  cant mitral regurgitation is a contraindication to PMV. nodes.title: Major trials in cardiology
nodes.summary:
The partial document provides an overview of major clinical trials in cardiology, detailing various studies that evaluate the efficacy and safety of different treatments for cardiovascular conditions. Key trials mentioned include:

1. **ACUITY** - Examines bivalirudin versus heparin plus glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in acute coronary syndromes, highlighting reduced bleeding with bivalirudin.
2. **ADMIRAL** - Assesses the impact of abciximab in primary angioplasty for myocardial infarction, showing improved outcomes with abciximab.
3. **AFCAPS/TexCAPS** - Investigates lovastatin for primary prevention of coronary events, demonstrating significant reductions in major acute coronary events.
4. **AFFIRM** - Compares rhythm control versus rate control in atrial fibrillation management, finding no significant mortality difference but noting more hospitalizations in the rhythm-control group.
5. **AHEFT** - Evaluates isosorbide dinitrate plus hydralazine in African American heart failure patients, showing improved mortality and reduced heart failure exacerbations.
6. **AIRE** - Studies ramipril's effect on mortality in AMI survivors with heart failure, reporting significant mortality reduction.
7. **ALLHAT** - Compares antihypertensive treatments in high-risk patients, finding no mortality difference but variations in blood pressure control.
8. **ASCOT-LLA** - Assesses atorvastatin's role in preventing coronary disease in hypertensive patients, showing significant reductions in cardiovascular events.
9. **ASSENT Trials** - Focus on the safety and efficacy of tenecteplase in acute myocardial infarction, with varying results on bleeding and mortality.
10. **BARI** - Compares CABG and PTCA in multivessel disease, concluding PTCA does not compromise survival compared to CABG, except in diabetics.

The document summarizes the purpose, methodology, follow-up duration, and key results of each trial, emphasizing their contributions to cardiology and patient care.

nodes.title: Cardiac Insufficiency Bisoprolol Study
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the efficacy of various medications and interventions in treating heart failure and coronary artery disease. Key trials highlighted include:

1. **Candesartan in Heart Failure**: Evaluated the effects of candesartan on all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations in patients with symptomatic heart failure across three trials (CHARM added, alternative, and preserved), showing a reduction in cardiovascular mortality and hospitalizations compared to placebo.

2. **CIBIS Trials**: The Cardiac Insufficiency Bisoprolol Study (CIBIS) and its follow-up (CIBIS II) assessed the impact of bisoprolol on heart failure patients, demonstrating significant reductions in hospitalizations but no significant mortality difference in the initial study, while CIBIS II showed lower all-cause mortality and hospital admissions.

3. **COMET Trial**: Compared carvedilol and metoprolol in heart failure patients, finding a 17% reduction in all-cause mortality with carvedilol.

4. **COM-PANION Trial**: Investigated the effects of optimal drug therapy alone versus combined with biventricular pacing or defibrillation in patients with heart failure and conduction delays, revealing significant reductions in mortality and hospitalization, particularly with the defibrillator.

5. **Carvedilol Prospective Randomized Cumulative Survival Trial**: Showed a 35% decrease in mortality in patients with severe heart failure treated with carvedilol.

6. **COPERNICUS Trial**: Focused on the efficacy of optimal medical therapy with or without percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in stable coronary artery disease, concluding no significant difference in mortality or myocardial infarction rates between the two treatment strategies over five years.

7. **COURAGE Trial**: Evaluated PCI versus optimal medical therapy in stable coronary artery disease, finding no difference in long-term outcomes, although PCI provided early benefits in angina relief.

Overall, the document summarizes the findings of these trials, emphasizing the importance of medication and intervention strategies in managing heart failure and coronary artery disease.

The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on their purposes, methodologies, and key results. 

1. **Carvedilol Prospective Randomized Cumulative Survival Trial**: This trial evaluated the effect of carvedilol on mortality in patients with severe heart failure, finding a 35% reduction in mortality compared to placebo over a mean follow-up of 10.4 months.

2. **COPERNICUS**: This study compared the efficacy of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with optimal medical therapy in patients with stable coronary artery disease. Results indicated no significant difference in mortality or myocardial infarction rates between the two treatments over 5 years, although PCI showed a temporary advantage in reducing angina.

3. **CREDO**: This trial assessed the benefits of long-term clopidogrel after PCI, revealing a 26.9% risk reduction in a composite endpoint of death, myocardial infarction, and stroke at one year for the clopidogrel group, with some benefit from pre-treatment with a loading dose.

4. **CTOPP**: This study compared physiological (dual chamber) and non-physiological (single chamber) pacemakers in patients requiring pacing for bradycardia. While there was no difference in cardiovascular death or stroke rates, physiological pacing significantly reduced the risk of developing atrial fibrillation.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of these trials in understanding treatment outcomes in heart failure, coronary artery disease, and pacing strategies.

The partial document covers several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the efficacy of various treatments for patients with coronary artery disease and related conditions. Key trials discussed include:

1. **CREDO Trial**: Evaluated the benefits of long-term clopidogrel after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) combined with aspirin. It involved 2,116 patients and found a 26.9% risk reduction in composite outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, stroke) at one year, particularly benefiting those who received a loading dose of clopidogrel more than 6 hours before the procedure.

2. **CTOPP Trial**: Compared physiological (dual chamber) pacemakers to non-physiological (single chamber) pacemakers in 1,474 patients. While there was no significant difference in cardiovascular death or stroke, the physiological pacing group showed a significant reduction in the risk of developing atrial fibrillation.

3. **Clopidogrel in Unstable Angina Study**: Investigated the impact of clopidogrel on 12,562 patients with acute coronary syndrome. The study reported a 20% reduction in the primary composite endpoint (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) and noted increased major bleeding in the clopidogrel group, although life-threatening bleeding rates were similar.

4. **DANAMI Trial**: Compared deferred invasive strategies (PCI or CABG) with conservative management in patients with inducible myocardial ischemia after thrombolysis for acute myocardial infarction. The invasive group had lower incidences of AMI and unstable angina, leading to recommendations for coronary angiography and potential revascularization in these patients.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of clopidogrel in managing coronary artery disease and the outcomes of different pacing strategies and invasive approaches in cardiac care.

CHAPTER 15 Major trials in cardiology 610
  CREDO Clopidogrel for Reduction of Events During ObservationPurpose: To evaluate the beneﬁ  t of long-term clopidogrel 
after PCI combined with aspirin, and to evaluate the beneﬁ  t of initiating clopidogrel with loading dose before 
the procedure. 2116 patients with symptomatic coronary artery disease and objective evidence of ischemia who were undergoing elective PCI or were deemed highly likely to undergo PCI were enrolled in 99 centers in North America. Patients were randomized to receive a 300 mg clopidogrel loading dose (n = 1053) or placebo ( n = 1063) 
3 to 24 hours before PCI. After the procedure, all patients received clopidogrel 75 mg/day for 28 days. From day 29 to 12 months, the loading-dose group received clopidogrel 75 mg/day, whereas placebo was given to the control group. The 1-year primary end point was a composite of death, myocardial infarction (MI), and stroke in the intent-to-treat population.Follow-up: 28 days, 6 months, and 1 yearResults: At 1 year, there was a 26.9% risk reduction in the combined end point of the clopidogrel-treated group. Pretreatment did not signiﬁ  cantly reduce the end point, but in a subgroup of patients receiving the loading dose more than 6 hours beforehand there was a signiﬁ  cant risk reduction.Reference: Steinhubl SR, et al. (2002) JAMA 288: 
2411–2420.
  CTOPP Canadian Trial Of Physiological PacingPurpose: To assess the potential beneﬁ  ts (measured by risk of cardiovascular death or stroke) of physiological (dual chamber) pacemakers compared with those of nonphysiological (single chamber) pacemakers over an extended period. 1474 patients requiring pacemakers for symptomatic bradycardia were randomized to receive one of the two modes of pacemaker.Follow-up: Initially 3 years, extended to a mean 6.4 yearsResults: There was no difference between groups in the primary outcome measures of cardiovascular death or stroke, or total mortality. However, there was a signiﬁ  cant reduction in the risk of developing atrial ﬁ  brillation in the physiological pacing group (relative risk reduction 20.1%, p  = 0.009).
Reference: Kerr CR, et al. (2004). Circulation 109:357–362.MAJOR TRIALS IN CARDIOLOGY 611
Clopidogrel in Unstable angina to prevent Recurrent EventsPurpose: To evaluate the impact of clopidogrel on 12,562 patients presenting within 24 hours of onset of acute coronary syndrome symptoms, either unstable angina (75%) or non-ST elevation MI (25%). Patients were randomized to receive 75 mg clopidogrel or placebo, preceded by 75–325 mg aspirin. There were similar rates of use of IV heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, ACE inhibitors, B-blockers, and lipid-lowering agents in the two 
groups.Follow-up: Mean 9 monthsResults: The clopidogrel group had a 20% overall reduction in the primary composite end point of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, and nonfatal stroke, and this beneﬁ  t 
was seen within 30 days. There was also a reduction in the incidence of refractory ischemia by 14% and severe ischemia by 24% in the clopidogrel group. All subgroups beneﬁ  ted from clopidogrel treatment. The incidence of 
major bleeding was 34% higher in the clopidogrel group (3.6% vs. 2.7%, p = 0.003), but life-threatening bleeding did 
not differ between the groups.Reference: CURE Study Investigators (2000). Eur J Cardiol 21:2033–2041.  CURE
Danish trial in Acute Myocardial InfarctionPurpose: To compare a deferred invasive strategy of PCI or CABG (n = 503, within 2–5 weeks of discharge) with a conservative strategy (n = 505) in patients with inducible myocardial ischemia (on exercise testing) within the ﬁ  rst 
few weeks after receiving thrombolysis for a ﬁ  rst AMI. 
Primary end points were death, AMI, and admission with unstable angina.Follow-up: 2.4 yearsResults: In the invasive group, PCI was given to 53% and CABG to 29%. Mortality was not signiﬁ  cantly different at 2.4 years between the invasive and conservative groups. However, the invasive group had a lower incidence of AMI, unstable angina, and stable angina. Therefore, the recommendation was to refer patients with inducible ischemia following AMI for a coronary angiogram ± revascularization.Reference: Madsen JK, et al. (1997). Circulation 96:
748–755.  DANAMI

nodes.title: COM-PANION Comparison of Medical Therapy, Pacing, and Defibrillation in Heart Failure Trial
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the efficacy of various treatments for acute coronary syndrome and myocardial infarction. Key points include:

1. **Clopidogrel in Unstable Angina**: A study involving 12,562 patients showed that clopidogrel, when combined with aspirin, significantly reduced the risk of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), and nonfatal stroke by 20%. It also reduced refractory and severe ischemia, although it was associated with a higher incidence of major bleeding.

2. **Danish Trial in Acute Myocardial Infarction**: This trial compared an invasive strategy (PCI or CABG) with a conservative approach in patients with inducible myocardial ischemia after thrombolysis for AMI. While mortality rates were similar, the invasive group experienced fewer instances of AMI and unstable angina, leading to recommendations for coronary angiography in such patients.

3. **DANAMI II Trial**: This trial evaluated the effectiveness of coronary angioplasty versus thrombolysis in AMI patients requiring transfer to a PCI-capable center. Results indicated that the invasive strategy was superior, with lower rates of the primary composite endpoint compared to thrombolysis, particularly in patients transferred within two hours.

4. **DAVID Trial**: This study assessed the efficacy of dual chamber pacing (DDDR) versus backup ventricular pacing (VVI) in patients with low left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and no bradycardia indications. The VVI group demonstrated better survival rates and fewer hospitalizations for heart failure, suggesting that DDDR may not provide additional benefits and could be detrimental in this patient population.

or stroke rates. 96% of patients were transferred from a community hospital to an invasive center within 2 hours. An invasive strategy is better than thrombolysis in patients at community hospitals if the transfer takes <2 hours.Reference: Henning R, et al. (2003). N Engl J Med 349:

pacing compared with backup ventricular pacing (VVI) in 506 patients with standard indications for ICD implantation but without indications for antibradycardia pacing. All had LVEF <40%, no bradycardia indications for pacing, and no persistent atrial arrhythmias. They were randomized to VVI at a backup rate of 40/min or DDDR at a backup rate of 70/min. hospitalization for CCF.Follow-up: 1 yearResults: The VVI group had 1-year survival-free rate of 83.9% vs. 73.3% for the DDDR group. nodes.title: Carvedilol Prospective Randomized Cumulative Survival Trial
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on different treatment strategies for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and heart failure. Key points include:

1. **DANAMI II Trial**: This trial compared coronary angioplasty with thrombolysis in AMI patients requiring transfer to a PCI-capable center. Results indicated that an invasive strategy (angioplasty) was superior to thrombolysis, particularly when transfer times were under two hours, with lower rates of reinfarction.

2. **DAVID Trial**: This study evaluated the efficacy of dual chamber pacing (DDDR) versus backup ventricular pacing (VVI) in patients with low left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and no bradycardia indications. The VVI group showed better survival rates and fewer hospitalizations for heart failure, suggesting that DDDR may not provide advantages in this patient population.

3. **Danish Investigations of Arrhythmia and Mortality on Dofetilide**: This trial assessed the prophylactic use of dofetilide in high-risk patients for sudden death. While there was no significant difference in overall mortality compared to placebo, dofetilide improved conversion rates to sinus rhythm in patients with atrial fibrillation.

4. **DIAMOND Trial**: This study investigated the effects of digoxin on all-cause mortality in heart failure patients. It found no reduction in overall mortality but noted a significant decrease in hospitalizations for worsening heart failure.

5. **DIGAMI Trial**: This trial examined the impact of insulin-glucose infusion in diabetic patients with AMI. The results showed a significant reduction in mortality, particularly in patients with a low cardiovascular risk profile.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of treatment strategies in managing AMI and heart failure, with varying outcomes based on the interventions studied.

nodes.title: COPERNICUS Optimal medical therapy with or without PCI for stable coronary disease
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the efficacy of various treatments in high-risk patient populations. Key trials include:

1. **Danish Investigations of Arrhythmia and Mortality On Dofetilide**: Evaluated dofetilide's prophylactic use in patients at high risk of sudden death, showing no significant mortality difference compared to placebo, but improved cardioversion rates in the CHF arm.

2. **Digitalis Investigation Group (DIG)**: Assessed digoxin's impact on all-cause mortality in heart failure patients, finding no mortality reduction but a significant decrease in hospitalizations for worsening heart failure.

3. **Diabetes mellitus Insulin-Glucose infusion in Acute Myocardial Infarction (DIGAMI)**: Investigated insulin-glucose infusion in diabetic patients with AMI, resulting in a notable reduction in mortality, particularly in those not previously on insulin.

4. **Defibrillator In Acute Myocardial Infarction Trial (DINAMIT)**: Explored the effects of prophylactic ICD therapy in high-risk post-MI patients, concluding no difference in all-cause mortality compared to medical therapy, although arrhythmic deaths were lower in the ICD group.

5. **European Myocardial Infarction Amiodarone Trial (EMIAT)**: Evaluated amiodarone's effect on mortality post-MI, finding no difference in overall mortality but a significant reduction in arrhythmic deaths.

6. **Evaluation in PTCA to Improve Long-term Outcome with abciximab (EPILOG)**: Aimed to determine the impact of abciximab during percutaneous coronary intervention on mortality and morbidity.

Overall, the document highlights the complexities of treatment outcomes in cardiology, emphasizing the need for tailored approaches based on patient profiles and conditions.

nodes.title: CREDO Clopidogrel for Reduction of Events During Observation
nodes.summary:
The partial document covers several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the evaluation of various treatments and their effects on mortality and morbidity in patients with acute myocardial infarction (MI) and other cardiovascular conditions. Key trials discussed include:

1. **DINAMIT Trial**: Investigated the impact of prophylactic implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) therapy in high-risk patients post-MI. The results showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality between ICD therapy and optimal medical therapy, although arrhythmic deaths were lower in the ICD group.

2. **EMIAT Trial**: Assessed the effect of amiodarone on mortality in patients with low left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) post-MI. The trial found no difference in all-cause or cardiac mortality, but a 35% reduction in arrhythmic deaths in the amiodarone group.

3. **EPILOG Trial**: Evaluated the use of abciximab, a glycoprotein receptor blocker, during percutaneous coronary intervention. The trial demonstrated a significant reduction in composite event rates without major bleeding differences, leading to its early termination due to positive results.

4. **EPISTENT Trial**: Focused on the influence of abciximab in patients undergoing stenting or balloon angioplasty, showing lower rates of death, MI, or urgent revascularization in the abciximab groups compared to placebo.

5. **ENHANCE Trial**: Compared the effects of ezetimibe-simvastatin versus high-dose simvastatin alone on carotid intima-media thickness in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia. The study found no significant differences in carotid IMT or clinical outcomes, although the combination therapy had a greater LDL-lowering effect.

Overall, the document highlights the complexities of treatment outcomes in cardiology, particularly regarding mortality and the effectiveness of various interventions.

The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the efficacy and safety of various treatments for cardiovascular conditions. Key points include:

1. **EPILOG Trial**: Evaluated the impact of abciximab on patients undergoing PTCA or stenting, showing a significant reduction in composite event rates without increased major bleeding risk, although minor bleeding was more common.

2. **EPISTENT Trial**: Investigated the effects of abciximab in stenting versus PTCA, finding lower rates of death, myocardial infarction (MI), or urgent revascularization in the abciximab groups compared to placebo.

3. **ENHANCE Trial**: Compared the effects of ezetimibe-simvastatin versus high-dose simvastatin alone on carotid intima-media thickness in patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, concluding no significant difference in IMT changes or clinical outcomes, despite greater LDL-lowering with the combination therapy.

4. **EUROPA Trial**: Assessed the effect of perindopril on cardiovascular risk in a low-risk population, demonstrating a 20% reduction in the primary endpoint of cardiovascular death, MI, or cardiac arrest compared to placebo.

5. **FRISC Trial**: Examined the addition of Fragmin in patients with unstable angina, finding reduced mortality and need for revascularization in the short term, although benefits did not persist long-term after treatment cessation.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of these trials in shaping treatment strategies for various cardiovascular diseases.

Evaluation of Platelet gpIIb/IIIa Inhibition in StentingPurpose: To evaluate the inﬂ  uence of platelet glycoprotein inhibitor cF7E3 on coronary disease treated by PTCA or stenting. Study design was randomized, double blinded, part placebo controlled. 2399 patients who were to undergo elective or urgent intervention, either balloon angioplasty alone or stenting, were randomized to receive abciximab or placebo. Aspirin and heparin were given to all patients, with ticlopidine given at physician’s discretion.Follow-up: 6 monthsResults: Death, MI, or need for urgent revascularization was lower within 30 days in both abciximab groups than with placebo. Within the abciximab group, these rates were lower in the stenting group than in the PTCA group alone. These trends were also observed at 6 months.Reference: Lincoff et al. (1999). Simvastatin with or without ezetimibe in familial hypercholesterolemiaPurpose: To compare the mean change in the intima-media thickness (IMT) measured at three sites in the carotid arteries between patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) treated with ezetimibe-simvastatin 10/80 mg vs. patients treated with high-dose simvastatin 80 mg alone, over a 2-year period. A total of 720 patients were enrolled with a mean age of 45.9 years. This was a randomized, double-blinded study.Follow-up: 24 monthsResults: They suggest that in patients with very high baseline LDL levels, such as those with HeFH, the combination of ezetimibe-simvastatin 10/80 mg does not result in signiﬁ  cant 
changes in mean carotid IMT at 2 years compared with high-dose simvastatin 80 mg alone. There was no difference in incidence of cardiovascular mortality, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and need for revascularization, although the study was not powered to study clinical outcomes. The incidence of adverse events was similar. The LDL-lowering effect of ezetimibe-simvastatin was greater than that with high-dose simvastatin alone.Reference: Kastelein JJ, et al. (2008). Concomitant treatment was with antiplatelet therapy (92%), B-blockers (62%), and lipid-lowering agents (58%). The primary end point was cardiovascular death, MI, or cardiac arrest.Follow-up: Mean 4.2 yearsResults: The primary end point was reached by 8% of the perindopril group and 10% of placebo ( p = 0.0003), 
representing a 20% risk reduction. Perindopril was well tolerated.Reference: The EUROPA Investigators (2003). Lancet 
362:782–788.
  FRISC Fragmin during Instability in Coronary Artery DiseasePurpose: To determine whether the addition of the low-molecular-weight heparin Fragmin (dalteparin) inﬂ  uences 
the recurrence of cardiac events in patients with unstable angina if added to aspirin and antianginal drugs. The study design was randomized, double blind, placebo controlled, parallel group. 1506 patients who were in the hospital with unstable angina within 72 hours of having chest pain were given either placebo or Fragmin 120 U/kg every 12 hours for the ﬁ  rst 6 days, then 7500 U once a day for 35–45 days 
thereafter. All patients were on aspirin and B-blockers (unless contraindicated), with calcium antagonists and nitrates as required.Follow-up: Up to 7 monthsResults: Mortality, need for revascularization, reinfarction, and need for IV heparin were lower in the ﬁ  rst 6 days in the Fragmin group. There was also a signiﬁ  cant reduction in the composite end point (death, revascularization, IV heparin use, MI), which persisted for up to 40 days for nonsmokers (80% of the sample), but this effect was not carried 4 to 5 months after the end of treatment in the group as a whole. If the dose of Fragmin was decreased, there was a risk of reinfarction that was greater in smokers.Reference: Fragmin during Instability in Coronary Artery Disease (FRISC) Study Group (1996). Lancet 347: 
561–568.

The partial document covers major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the evaluation of various treatments for cardiovascular conditions. Key trials discussed include:

1. **EUROPA Trial**: Investigated the effects of perindopril on cardiovascular risk in a low-risk population with stable coronary artery disease. The study found a 20% risk reduction in cardiovascular events among patients receiving perindopril compared to placebo.

2. **FRISC Trial**: Assessed the impact of the low-molecular-weight heparin Fragmin on patients with unstable angina. Results indicated that Fragmin reduced mortality and the need for revascularization in the short term, although benefits diminished after treatment ended.

3. **FRISC II Trial**: Compared invasive and non-invasive strategies in unstable angina patients, finding that early revascularization led to fewer deaths and myocardial infarctions, regardless of Fragmin treatment.

4. **GISSI-I Trial**: Evaluated the efficacy of streptokinase in reducing in-hospital and one-year mortality after acute myocardial infarction (AMI), showing significant mortality reduction, especially when treatment was administered within three hours of symptom onset.

5. **GISSI-2 Trial**: Compared streptokinase and alteplase in AMI patients, focusing on the effects of heparin post-thrombolysis on survival and post-ischemic events.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of these trials in shaping treatment strategies for cardiovascular diseases.

nodes.title: Danish trial in Acute Myocardial Infarction
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the evaluation of various treatments for patients with unstable angina and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Key points include:

1. **Fragmin and Revascularization during Instability in Coronary Artery Disease**: This trial assessed the effects of Fragmin (dalteparin) in patients with unstable angina, comparing an invasive strategy to a non-invasive approach. Results indicated fewer deaths and myocardial infarctions in the invasive group after 6 months.

2. **GISSI-I Trial**: This study evaluated the impact of streptokinase (SK) on in-hospital and 1-year mortality after AMI. It found an 18% reduction in mortality at 21 days and a 17.2% mortality rate at 12 months in the SK group compared to controls.

3. **GISSI-2 Trial**: This trial compared SK and alteplase (rt-PA) in AMI patients, examining the effects of heparin on survival and complications. No significant differences were found in mortality or complications, although major bleeding was more frequent with SK.

4. **GISSI-3 Trial**: This study investigated the effects of lisinopril and nitrates on survival and left ventricular function after AMI. Lisinopril significantly reduced mortality and left ventricular dysfunction, while nitrates did not affect outcomes.

5. **GISSI-Prevenzione Trial**: This trial evaluated the impact of dietary supplements (n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and vitamin E) after MI. While vitamin E showed no benefit, PUFA resulted in a significant reduction in cardiovascular events, particularly in mortality rates.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of various pharmacological interventions in improving outcomes for patients with coronary artery disease and AMI.

combined end point of death and severe left ventricular damage, rates of in-hospital complications (15 days post thrombolysis), or rates of reinfarction in all groups, with or without heparin. Major bleeding occurred more frequently in the SK plus heparin group, but stroke rates were similar in all groups (1.14%); rt-PA was associated with a small but excess risk of stroke. nodes.title: DANAMI II Danish trial in Acute Myocardial Infarction II
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the outcomes of various treatments for acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Key trials highlighted include:

1. **GISSI-2**: Evaluated the effects of streptokinase (SK) with or without heparin on mortality and complications post-thrombolysis. Results showed no significant differences in mortality or reinfarction rates, but higher major bleeding rates were noted with SK plus heparin.

2. **GISSI-3**: Investigated the impact of lisinopril and nitrates on survival and left ventricular (LV) function in AMI patients. Lisinopril significantly reduced mortality and LV dysfunction at 6 weeks, while nitrates did not affect outcomes.

3. **GISSI-Prevenzione**: Assessed the effects of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) and vitamin E on post-MI outcomes. PUFA showed a significant reduction in cardiovascular events, while vitamin E had no impact.

4. **Global Utilization of Streptokinase and t-PA**: Compared the efficacy of different thrombolytic treatments in AMI. The accelerated t-PA regimen resulted in lower mortality and complications compared to SK-only treatments, although older patients had higher mortality rates.

5. **GUSTO-1**: Focused on the long-term effects of abciximab in patients with acute coronary syndrome. The study found no survival benefit from abciximab, with some subgroups experiencing higher mortality.

Overall, the document summarizes the findings of these trials, emphasizing the effectiveness and safety of various pharmacological interventions in managing AMI and their implications for patient outcomes.

nodes.title: DAVID Dual chamber And VVI Implantable Defibrillator
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses several major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the effectiveness of various treatments for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Key points include:

1. **Global Utilization of Streptokinase and t-PA**: This trial compared the effects of different treatment regimens involving streptokinase (SK) and tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) on mortality rates in AMI patients. Results indicated that the accelerated t-PA regimen significantly reduced mortality compared to SK-only treatments, although it was associated with a higher incidence of hemorrhagic strokes.

2. **GUSTO-1 Trial**: This study evaluated the long-term effects of abciximab in ACS patients without ST elevation. It found no survival benefit from abciximab, with some subgroups experiencing higher mortality rates.

3. **HOPE Trial**: This trial assessed the impact of the ACE inhibitor ramipril and vitamin E on high-risk cardiovascular patients. Ramipril significantly reduced the incidence of major cardiovascular events and total mortality, particularly in diabetic patients, while vitamin E showed no significant benefits.

4. **HORIZONS-AMI Trial**: This ongoing trial aims to compare bivalirudin with heparin plus glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for STEMI.

Overall, the document highlights the importance of these trials in shaping treatment strategies for cardiovascular diseases and their varying impacts on patient outcomes.

  HOPE Heart Outcomes Prevention Evaluation TrialPurpose: To assess the role of the ACE inhibitor ramipril and vitamin E in patients at high risk of cardiovascular events who did not have LV dysfunction or heart failure. 9297 patients >55 years old with evidence of vascular disease (previous MI, angina, multivessel PTCA or CABG, multivessel coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease) or diabetes plus one other risk factor but not known to have a low LV EF or heart failure were randomly assigned to receive 10 mg ramipril (titrated up from 2.5 mg) or placebo, plus vitamin E 400 U/day or placebo. Primary outcome was composite of MI, stroke, or death from cardiovascular events. Secondary end points were death from any cause, need for revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure, and complications of diabetes. Patients had approximately similar usage of aspirin, B-blockers, lipid-
lowering agents, diuretics, and calcium channel blockers in the two groups.Follow-up: Mean 5 yearsResults: More people in the ramipril group stopped treatment due to cough, hypotension, or dizziness. However, there was a signiﬁ  cant reduction in the primary end points of MI, stroke, and death compared to placebo (14% vs. 17%), as well a reduction in total mortality. There was no signiﬁ  cant reduction in noncardiovascular death. In the ramipril group there was signiﬁ  cantly less need for revascularization, fewer complications of diabetes, less heart failure or worsening angina, and smaller incidence of new-onset diabetes. The reduction in the primary end point and cardiovascular death was even more striking in diabetics (15.3% vs. 19.6%). There was a clear beneﬁ  t in 
the ramipril group in patients with or without evidence of coronary artery disease, with or without history of MI and EF >40%. Beneﬁ  ts were also seen whether or not patients were taking aspirin, B-blockers, lipid-lowering agents, or anti-hypertensive drugs. In the vitamin E group there were no signiﬁ  cant differences in primary or secondary end points. The study was stopped 6 months early due to consistent observed beneﬁ  ts in primary end points.Reference: Yusuf S, et al. (2000). N Engl J Med 342: 
145–153.

nodes.title: Danish Investigations of Arrhythmia and Mortality On Dofetilide
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on three significant studies: the HOPE trial, HORIZONS-AMI trial, and the Heart Protection Study. 

1. **HOPE Trial**: This trial evaluated the effects of the ACE inhibitor ramipril and vitamin E on patients over 55 years old at high risk for cardiovascular events. The study found that ramipril significantly reduced the primary composite outcomes of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and cardiovascular death compared to placebo, with additional benefits observed in diabetic patients. The trial was stopped early due to consistent benefits.

2. **HORIZONS-AMI Trial**: This trial compared bivalirudin with heparin plus gpIIb/IIIa inhibitors in patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). CHAPTER 15 Major trials in cardiology 620
  HOPE Heart Outcomes Prevention Evaluation TrialPurpose: To assess the role of the ACE inhibitor ramipril and vitamin E in patients at high risk of cardiovascular events who did not have LV dysfunction or heart failure. 9297 patients >55 years old with evidence of vascular disease (previous MI, angina, multivessel PTCA or CABG, multivessel coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease) or diabetes plus one other risk factor but not known to have a low LV EF or heart failure were randomly assigned to receive 10 mg ramipril (titrated up from 2.5 mg) or placebo, plus vitamin E 400 U/day or placebo. Primary outcome was composite of MI, stroke, or death from cardiovascular events. Secondary end points were death from any cause, need for revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure, and complications of diabetes. Patients had approximately similar usage of aspirin, B-blockers, lipid-
lowering agents, diuretics, and calcium channel blockers in the two groups.Follow-up: Mean 5 yearsResults: More people in the ramipril group stopped treatment due to cough, hypotension, or dizziness. However, there was a signiﬁ  cant reduction in the primary end points of MI, stroke, and death compared to placebo (14% vs. 17%), as well a reduction in total mortality. There was no signiﬁ  cant reduction in noncardiovascular death. In the ramipril group there was signiﬁ  cantly less need for revascularization, fewer complications of diabetes, less heart failure or worsening angina, and smaller incidence of new-onset diabetes. The reduction in the primary end point and cardiovascular death was even more striking in diabetics (15.3% vs. 19.6%). There was a clear beneﬁ  t in 
the ramipril group in patients with or without evidence of coronary artery disease, with or without history of MI and EF >40%. Beneﬁ  ts were also seen whether or not patients were taking aspirin, B-blockers, lipid-lowering agents, or anti-hypertensive drugs. In the vitamin E group there were no signiﬁ  cant differences in primary or secondary end points. The study was stopped 6 months early due to consistent observed beneﬁ  ts in primary end points.Reference: Yusuf S, et al. (2000). N Engl J Med 342: 
145–153.

Follow-up: 1 yearResults: Among patients undergoing planned primary PCI for acute MI, use of bivalirudin was associated with a reduction in the composite end point of death, MI, target vessel revascularization, stroke, or major bleeding at 30 days compared with heparin plus gpIIb/IIIa inhibitors. This ﬁ  nding was driven by a reduction in major bleeding, with no difference in MACE. There was still a signiﬁ  cantly 
reduced incidence of the composite end point at 12 months, but in addition to bleeding, a signiﬁ  cant reduction 
in mortality and non–Q-wave MI was also noted. There was an increase in early (<24 hours) stent thrombosis with the use of bivalirudin; however, there was no difference between study arms at the end of 1 year.Reference: Stone GW, et al. (2008). N Engl J Med 358: 
2218–2230.  HORIZONS-AMI
Heart Protection StudyPurpose: To evaluate whether the lowering of blood concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), irrespective of the initial cholesterol measure, is associated with a lower cardiovascular risk. 20,536 patients with coronary disease, other occlusive arterial disease, or diabetes were randomized to 40 mg simvastatin once daily or placebo. The average compliance in the statin group was 85%, and in the placebo group the average non-study statin use was 17%. Primary outcome measures were death, and fatal or nonfatal vascular events.Follow-up: 5 yearsResults: All-cause mortality was signiﬁ  cantly reduced 
in the simvastatin group (12.9% vs. 14.7%, p = 0.0003) mainly due to an 18% reduction in the coronary death rate. There was a marginal reduction in other vascular deaths, and no signiﬁ  cant reduction in nonvascular deaths. There was a signiﬁ  cant reduction in the ﬁ  rst-event rate 
for nonfatal MI or coronary death, nonfatal or fatal stroke, and for coronary revascularization. The proportional reduction in event rate was similar in each subcategory—that is, those with diagnosed coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes; and separately, in women; in those whose presenting LDL-C was <3.0 mmol/L or total cholesterol <5 mmol/L. The beneﬁ  ts of simvastatin were in addition to existing treatments. There was a 0.01 annual excess risk of myopathy, and there were no signiﬁ  cant adverse effects on cancer incidence or hospitalization for any nonvascular causes.Reference: Heart Protection Study Collaborative Group (2002). (2005). N Engl J Med 353: 1095–1104.
  ISAR REACTA clinical trial of abciximab in elective percutaneous coronary intervention after pretreatment with clopidogrelPurpose: To evaluate whether treatment with gpIIb/IIIa inhibitor abciximab reduces postprocedure ischemic complications in low-risk patients pretreated with clopidogrel who undergo coronary stenting. A total of 2159 patients were enrolled with a mean age of 66 years. MAJOR TRIALS IN CARDIOLOGY 623
Follow-up: Mean 30-day follow-upResults: In low-risk patients with coronary disease pretreated with high-dose clopidogrel and undergoing elective coronary stenting, treatment with the gpIIb/IIIa inhibitor abciximab was not associated with a reduction in the primary composite end point of death, MI, or urgent TVR at 30 days. The trial patient population was at very low risk, excluding patients with insulin-dependent diabetes, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and positive biomarkers. First International Study of Infarct SurvivalPurpose: To assess the impact on mortality of early use of B-blockers (atenolol 5–10 mg IV over 5 minutes followed by 100 mg orally once daily for 7 days) randomized in 16,027 patients with acute MI (<12 hours), in the ﬁ  rst week 
and after longer follow-up.Follow-up: Mean 20 monthsResults: In the ﬁ  rst 7 days, there was a 15% reduction (p < 
0.02) in vascular deaths in the atenolol group, with greatest beneﬁ  t on day 1, due to reduction in acute myocardial 
rupture. A further reduction in deaths was observed after 1 year.Reference: Randomized trial of intravenous atenolol among 16027 cases of suspected acute myocardial infarction: ISIS-1. Lancet 1986; ii:57–66.  ISIS-1

There was a 25% odds reduction in death with streptokinase and 23% odds reduction with aspirin. There was a 42% odds reduction in death with aspirin and streptokinase combined, compared to the placebo group. Streptokinase was associated with more bleeding requiring blood transfusion (0.5% vs. 0.2% in placebo group) but fewer strokes (0.6% vs. 0.8% in placebo group). nodes.title: ISIS-2 Second International Study of Infarct Survival
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses major clinical trials in cardiology, focusing on the efficacy of various treatments for patients with coronary disease and acute myocardial infarction (MI). It highlights the results of three significant trials:

1. A trial assessing the use of the gpIIb/IIIa inhibitor abciximab in low-risk patients undergoing elective coronary stenting, which found no reduction in the primary composite endpoint of death, MI, or urgent target vessel revascularization (TVR) at 30 days.

2. The First International Study of Infarct Survival (ISIS-1), which evaluated the early use of intravenous atenolol in patients with acute MI. The results indicated a 15% reduction in vascular deaths within the first week, particularly on day 1, and a further reduction in mortality observed after one year.

3. The Second International Study of Infarct Survival (ISIS-2), which examined the effects of intravenous streptokinase and oral aspirin in patients with suspected AMI. The study reported significant reductions in mortality with both treatments, especially when combined, while also noting the associated risks of bleeding and nonfatal reinfarction.

Overall, the document summarizes the findings and implications of these trials for treatment strategies in cardiology.

structure.title: Special populations: women and elderly
structure.summary:
The partial document covers a series of major clinical trials in cardiology, detailing their purposes, methodologies, follow-up durations, and key results. It includes findings from trials assessing various treatments for conditions such as acute myocardial infarction (AMI), unstable angina, heart failure, and the effects of different medications and interventions on cardiovascular outcomes. 

Key points include:

1. **Clopidogrel and Abciximab**: In low-risk coronary disease patients, abciximab did not reduce major adverse cardiovascular events compared to placebo.
2. **B-blockers in AMI**: Early use of atenolol showed a significant reduction in vascular deaths within the first week of treatment.
3. **Streptokinase and Aspirin**: The combination of streptokinase and aspirin significantly reduced mortality in suspected AMI patients.
4. **Heparin and Thrombolytics**: The addition of heparin to thrombolytic therapy showed mixed results in mortality and bleeding risks.
5. **Rosuvastatin**: This medication significantly reduced cardiovascular events in patients with elevated C-reactive protein but normal LDL levels.
6. **Losartan vs. Atenolol**: Losartan showed lower all-cause mortality compared to atenolol in patients with diabetes and hypertension.
7. **ICD Trials**: The MADIT trials demonstrated significant mortality reductions with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators in high-risk patients.
8. **Heart Failure Treatments**: Trials like MERIT-HF and MIRACLE evaluated the benefits of metoprolol and cardiac resynchronization therapy, respectively, showing significant improvements in mortality and quality of life.
9. **Stroke Prevention**: The PROGRESS trial highlighted the effectiveness of perindopril in reducing stroke risk in patients with a history of transient ischemic attacks or strokes.
10. **Pacing Trials**: Studies like MOST and PASE assessed the impact of different pacing strategies on quality of life and clinical outcomes in patients with bradycardia and heart failure.

Overall, the document summarizes the efficacy and safety of various pharmacological and device-based interventions in improving cardiovascular health outcomes across different patient populations.
